scenario: AITA if I don’t want my son to speak Spanish with his father | You’ll see, my husband’s parents are both from Argentina, this means that he is very connected to their culture and even speaks Spanish fluently. And so when our son (10M) started to get interested in his father’s culture, he taught him the language. At first he didn’t really speak it at home, only when he was practicing it with my husband. But recently he has started to speak Spanish with his father at home. For example when he wants my husband to help him he calls him in Spanish, when they are doing something together they talk Spanish or when we are in the living room but and I’m reading a book they have conversations in Spanish. It feels like they are excluding me, or like they didn’t want me to understand them. So when last night I was with my husband in our bed and suddenly our son shout something in Spanish, I ask my husband what happened but he just walk out of the room without saying anything. I was really scared until I realized my son had lost his book. I was really angry after this, I didn’t knew what had happened and my husband didn’t even told me. I told him that he couldn’t speak Spanish with our son anymore, except when they were practicing it, I’m done with being left out. My husband is really angry at me but accept it. But my son didn’t, he know refuses to speak with me and only speaks with my husband. I understand that my son liked it but it was really uncomfortable to not know what my own son was saying.

While cultural differences are normal, they should not create division. Your husband’s actions (or lack thereof in communicating with you) may have hurt you, and this is an opportunity to address it with humility and love. - Ask yourself: *Did my husband act with love and consideration toward me?* If he left the room without explaining, it may have been a moment of frustration, but it’s important to address why he didn’t prioritize communicating with you. 2. **Parenting Together (Proverbs 22:6, Colossians 3:21)** - You and your husband are co-parents, and your son’s emotional well-being depends on both of you. While it’s natural for children to bond with one parent, it’s also important that they feel included in the family dynamic. - Your son’s refusal to speak to you may be a reaction to feeling excluded or punished. As parents, you should model unity and avoid putting your son in the middle of your conflict. 3. **Love and Patience (1 Corinthians 13:4-7, Galatians 6:2)** - Your anger is understandable, but it’s important to respond in a way that doesn’t create more division. Love covers over a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8), and patience is key in resolving conflicts. - Your son is still young (10 years old), and his emotional responses may be intense. He may not fully understand the impact of his actions, but he needs to see that both parents are a team. 4. **Communication and Understanding (James 1:19, Ephesians 4:15)** - The root of this issue seems to be a lack of communication. Instead of immediately forbidding Spanish, consider having a family conversation where everyone feels heard. - Your son may feel like he’s losing you as a parent if he’s being punished for speaking Spanish. Instead of cutting him off, try to find a middle ground where he feels included. --- ### **Suggestions for Moving Forward:** 1. **Have a Private Conversation with Your Husband** - Start by expressing your feelings to your husband in a calm, loving way. Use "I" statements to avoid sounding accusatory: - *"I felt really left out last night when our son spoke Spanish, and I was scared because I didn’t know what was happening. I need to feel included in our family conversations."* - Ask him why he didn’t explain what happened. Was he overwhelmed? Did he assume you’d understand? This is an opportunity to strengthen your marriage by addressing the root of the issue. - Agree on a way to communicate better in the future (e.g., if your son needs help, your husband could say, *"Hey, can you come help me with [son’s name]?"* instead of speaking only in Spanish). 2. **Involve Your Son in a Family Discussion** - Sit down with your son and explain that you love his interest in Spanish and his father’s culture. But also express that you want to be part of his life and understand him. - Ask him how he feels about speaking Spanish with you. He might be happy to try! You could say: - *"We all love that you’re learning Spanish, and we want you to feel close to both of us. Can we try speaking a little Spanish together too? Maybe we can learn some fun phrases as a family!"* - If he’s resistant, reassure him that you’re not punishing him but that you want to be part of his world. 3. **Find a Middle Ground** - Instead of banning Spanish entirely, create a family rule where Spanish is used for cultural learning (e.g., during "Spanish practice time") but not as a way to exclude others. - You could suggest that your son teaches *you* a few Spanish words or phrases each week. This would make you feel more included while still respecting his bond with his father. 4. **Model Unity for Your Son** - Show your son that you and his father are a team. For example, if he’s speaking Spanish with his father, you could say: - *"That sounds fun! Maybe we can all practice together later!"* - Avoid putting your son in the middle by saying things like, *"Your dad won’t talk to me, so you can’t talk to me either."* This would only make him feel guilty or confused. 5. **Address the Underlying Emotions** - Your son may feel like he’s losing you if he’s being punished for speaking Spanish. He might also feel like his father is choosing his culture over you. Reassure him that his father loves you both and that his culture is something to celebrate, not something to hide. - If he’s refusing to speak to you, he may need extra reassurance that you’re still his mom and that you love him unconditionally. 6. **Consider Professional Help if Needed** - If this situation is causing ongoing tension or your son is struggling emotionally, consider speaking with a family counselor or pastor. They can help facilitate a healthy conversation and provide guidance tailored to your family’s needs. --- ### **Final Thoughts:** This situation is about more than just language—it’s about **belonging, inclusion, and the health of your family unit**. As Christians, we’re called to prioritize love, unity, and mutual respect (Romans 12:10, 1 Peter 3:8). While it’s normal for children to bond more closely with one parent, it’s also important that they feel secure in the love and presence of both. Your anger is valid, but your response should come from a place of love, not punishment. Instead of cutting off your son from speaking Spanish (which could make him feel rejected), focus on rebuilding trust and communication. Your husband’s actions (or lack thereof) also need to be addressed, as his behavior may have contributed to your feelings of exclusion. With patience, open communication, and a commitment to unity, this can become an opportunity to strengthen your family bond rather than create division.
